Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which stanza in Audre Lorde's poem "Father Son and Holy Ghost" has indented lines. I remember that in poetry, indentation can be used to create a visual break, often for emphasis or to separate stanzas. But first, I need to get my hands on the actual text of the poem to check for any indented lines.

I started by searching online for the full text of the poem. I went to the Poetry Foundation website, but when I tried to access the specific page, it gave me a 404 error. That was frustrating because I really needed the text. Then I tried other search queries like "Audre Lorde Father Son and Holy Ghost full text read" and "Audre Lorde Father Son and Holy Ghost poem PDF," but none of these searches gave me the complete poem. Some results mentioned the poem but didn't provide the full text.

I also checked the Wikisource page for the poem, but it turned out to be a hymn by Charles Wesley, not Lorde's work. That was confusing because I was looking for Lorde's specific poem. I even tried looking at educational resources and literary databases, but again, I couldn't find the full text.

After several failed attempts, I realized that the issue was that the correct page wasn't accessible. The links I found either led to broken pages or didn't have the full poem. This made it impossible to analyze the stanzas for indentation. I kept trying different search terms, but each time, I ended up with the same problem—either partial text or broken links.

I think the main mistake here was that the WebSurfer agent didn't refine its search strategy enough. It kept trying the same or similar search queries without considering that the Poetry Foundation page might be down or the links might be outdated. Without being able to access the full text, I couldn't proceed to identify the stanza with indented lines.

So, the error occurred because the WebSurfer agent didn't effectively validate or refine its search results, leading to repeated failures in retrieving the necessary information. This prevented the task from being completed as intended.
